A barber named Elias Moreno noticed it first. He was cutting Mr. Hollis's neck on Tuesday morning and saw his reflection holding the scissors half a second late. Just a lag, like a bad video call. He stopped. His reflection stopped after him. By Thursday it was everywhere—people filming themselves in mirrors, posting confused clips. Delay kept growing. Half a second became a full second, two seconds. Scientists on TV with careful faces said "optical anomaly," which everyone knew meant they had no idea.

What nobody knew was mirrors weren't reflecting anything. They were windows. Another Earth on the other side, perfect copy, left and right swapped. For all of history the two worlds moved in perfect lockstep. Every gesture matched. Until something over there slipped. Maybe an atom decayed wrong. Maybe a butterfly flapped the wrong way. The two worlds started drifting and it kept accelerating.

Two weeks in, people weren't just seeing delays. They were seeing different things. A woman in Ohio watched her reflection brush its teeth while she stood still. A teenager in Seoul saw his reflection walk out of frame, leaving an empty bedroom behind the glass. Elias hung sheets over his mirrors. So did most people.

One evening he lifted the corner. His reflection was sitting in the barber chair facing him. It looked tired, had stubble Elias didn't have, messier shop. It held up paper with backward handwriting: YOU SEE IT TOO?

Elias grabbed a pen and wrote backward on a receipt, the way he used to do as a kid for fun: YES.

His reflection laughed. He'd never seen himself laugh from the outside. Strange sound to watch without hearing.

They talked for hours with paper to the glass. The other Elias said his world was scared too. His scientists had careful faces. His mirrors were covered.

DO YOU THINK IT STOPS? the other wrote.

Elias thought about all the years looking into mirrors, never once thinking someone was looking back.

I DON'T KNOW. BUT COME BACK TOMORROW.

The next night the other Elias was waiting. So was he. As the two worlds kept drifting apart, two barbers kept meeting at the glass, holding up their backward letters, trying to stay in sync on purpose.

They called it Halcyon, and for nineteen days it was perfect. On day twenty the first people didn't wake up. By month's end the ones still alive were screaming, and not random—at windows, at spoons, at dark phone screens. Anything that could hold a reflection.

I got my shot the first morning in a high school gym. Yellow sun sticker. I thought I was lucky. Still do mostly. Haven't died. Haven't screamed. Six weeks in a silent city, stepping over broken glass, telling myself it just missed me like lightning misses most people. But I've been careful. Shaved by feel. Taped a towel over my bathroom mirror the day my neighbor went through hers.

This morning I pulled the towel down. My face was there. Thinner, unshaven, bloodshot, but mine. I almost laughed. I lifted my hand to touch my stubble and the guy in the mirror lifted his. A fraction late. I went still. He went still too, a heartbeat after, and I understood what the others saw. Not a monster. Just patience: something calm and patient that spent six weeks learning to be me. Slowly I lowered my hand. He didn't.

text:
A lot of countries spend huge money on space. Rockets to the Moon and Mars, big telescopes. But some people think that money should go to Earth problems—poverty, hunger, climate change. I think both matter, but governments should fix Earth problems first.

So many people don't have food or clean water. Kids can't go to school because their families are too poor. It's sad seeing that on the news. We spend billions on Mars while people starve. If governments used that money for hospitals, schools, clean water, a lot of lives would be saved.

Earth has serious environment problems too. Climate's changing, weather getting more extreme. Floods, fires, crazy heat. Scientists say we need to act fast. I think protecting Earth is more urgent than exploring other planets. Earth's the only home we have right now.

But I get why space exploration matters too. A lot of tech we use every day came from space research—GPS, weather satellites, medical equipment. Satellites help us watch climate change and predict storms. So space programs aren't just about other planets, they help people on Earth.

Plus space exploration gets young people excited about science. I watched astronaut videos when I was a kid and wanted to be one. Space programs can inspire students to study hard and become scientists or engineers.

So I don't think governments should stop space exploration, because it gives us useful tech and inspiration. But they should spend most of the money on Earth problems—hunger, poverty, environment. If we take care of our planet first, then we can explore space with better conditions. Balance is the answer.

text:
I could see it in their looks and the way they smiled. They knew.

Thanksgiving at Aunt Carol's is always the same: turkey smell since dawn, football in the den, cousins fighting over the good chair. This year the smells and sounds were the same but the moment I walked in, every conversation stopped for one heartbeat too long.

"Danny!" Carol said, smile that didn't reach her eyes. "You made it."

"I made it," I said.

She hugged me like I was a bomb.

I'd told one person: my mom. Three weeks ago, after wine, I said, "Mom, I quit law school." Long silence. "Okay. We'll talk about it." She'd apparently told everyone in the tri-state area.

Uncle Ray asked "How's school?" and then his eyes went to my mom, suddenly very interested in cranberry sauce.

"It's fine," I said.

Grandma patted the couch. "Sit, sweetheart. Tell me what you're doing." Voice like talking to a horse that might bolt.

Across the room Megan, who passed the bar exam first try and never shut up about it, looked at me with so much pity I wanted to crawl under the carpet.

For two hours it was like this. Nobody said it. Everyone circled it. Ray told a story about some guy's son who "found his passion" after "a few false starts." Carol mentioned "plenty of successful people changed direction." Grandpa, eighty-nine and mostly deaf, yelled "Is this the one who flunked out?" and the room went dead quiet until Carol said the rolls were ready.

I didn't flunk out. I left. Different thing, though nobody at that table heard it.

At dinner Mom caught my eye. She looked miserable. She'd been asking for help. Asking everyone what to say to me.

I put my fork down.

"Okay. I quit law school. You all know. I'd rather just talk about it than have everyone be weird all night. I wasn't happy. I was good at it, but wasn't happy. I'm working at a woodshop in Easton. Building furniture. Learning. I'm okay."

Nobody moved. Then Grandpa, who heard everything for once, said, "Furniture?"

"Furniture," I said.

He nodded. "My father built furniture. Best man I ever knew."

Just like that, the room breathed. Ray asked what kind of wood I like. Megan admitted she hates her firm. Carol asked if I could fix her wobbly dining chair she's been threatening to throw out for years.

Mom didn't say anything. Just squeezed my hand under the table.

The looks stayed the rest of the night but different now. Not hooded. Curious. Smiles real.

Walking out, Carol handed me a bag of leftovers and the wobbly chair.

"No pressure," she said.

I laughed. So did she.
